entry: Branch of industry that develops and produces industrial, specialty and other chemicals. Central to the modern world economy, it converts raw materials such as oil, natural gas, air, water, metals and minerals into commodity chemicals. Its branches include [[Petrochemical|petrochemicals]] such as [[Polymer|polymers]] for [[Plastic|plastics]] and synthetic fibers, inorganic acids and alkalis, and agricultural chemicals such as [[Fertilizer|fertilizers]] and [[Pesticide|pesticides]]. The heavy chemical industry coincided with the beginnings of the [[Industrial Revolution]]. In 1736 Joshua Ward developed a process for producing [[Sulfuric acid]] on a large scale, and Charles Tennant's bleaching powder spurred the first great chemical enterprise, the St Rollox Chemical Works north of [[Glasgow]]. By the 1870s British soda output of 200,000 tons annually exceeded that of all other nations combined.

Branch of [[Physical chemistry]] concerned with the rates of [[Chemical reaction|chemical reactions]]. Unlike [[Thermodynamics|thermodynamics]], which indicates the direction a reaction takes but says nothing about its rate, kinetics examines how the physical state of reactants, their concentrations, [[Temperature]] and catalysts influence reaction speed, and it reveals the [[Reaction mechanism|reaction mechanism]]. Ludwig Wilhelmy studied the rate of sucrose inversion in 1850. In 1864 Peter Waage and Cato Guldberg published the law of mass action, which states that reaction speed is proportional to the quantity of reacting substances. Van 't Hoff, who published *Études de dynamique chimique* in 1884, received the first Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1901. Activation energy is determined through the [[Arrhenius equation]].

Industrial process plant that manufactures or otherwise processes chemicals, usually on a large scale. Its general objective is to create new material wealth through the chemical or biological transformation or separation of materials, using specialized equipment, units and technology. Feedstock, the raw material fed into a plant, is converted into products through steps called unit operations carried out in interconnected units, in either continuous or batch operation. Batch production is common in pharmaceutical and specialty chemicals for its traceability and flexibility, while continuous plants usually make commodity or [[Petrochemical|petrochemicals]]. Petrochemical plants are usually located next to an [[Oil refinery|oil refinery]] to minimize feedstock transport costs. Explosions, fires and toxic releases have occurred at chemical plants, prompting stringent safety regulations.

Artificial execution of [[Chemical reaction|chemical reactions]] to obtain one or more products. Reagents, or reactants, undergo transformation under set conditions, and many reactions require a work-up or purification step to isolate the final product. Yield is expressed as a mass in grams in a [[Laboratory|laboratory]] setting, or as a percentage of the theoretical quantity based on the limiting reagent, and a side reaction can reduce it. Multistep synthesis requires a separate work-up for each stage; the synthesis of [[Paracetamol]] typically needs three reactions. One-pot synthesis carries out several reactions in one vessel without isolating intermediates. Organic synthesis, a major branch of the field, builds [[Organic compound|organic compounds]] from basic lab compounds or modifies natural products.

Specialized munition that uses chemicals formulated to inflict death or harm on humans. Lethal agents include nerve agents such as sarin and VX and blister agents such as mustard gas, while non-lethal ones include tear gases. Under the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons definition, toxic chemicals used for other properties, such as the herbicide [[Agent Orange]], are excluded. Chemical weapons were first used on a large scale in World War I. [[Nazi Germany]] used [[Hydrogen cyanide|hydrogen cyanide]] in gas chambers to commit genocide against [[Jews]] during [[World War II]], and [[The Holocaust|the Holocaust]] had the largest death toll from chemical weapons in history. They were repeatedly used in the [[Iran–Iraq War]] and the [[Syrian civil war]]. The 1993 Chemical Weapons Convention prohibits their production, stockpiling and use, and as of 2025 it had 193 state parties.

[[Cancer]] treatment using one or more anti-cancer drugs in a standard regimen. It may aim for cure, usually with drug combinations, or only to prolong life or reduce symptoms. Chemotherapy drugs inhibit [[Mitosis|cell division]] or induce DNA damage, and as systemic therapy they reach cancer anywhere in the body, often alongside [[Radiation therapy|radiation]] or [[Surgery|surgery]]. Because they also damage rapidly dividing healthy cells, such as those in bone marrow, the digestive tract and hair follicles, common side effects include myelosuppression, mucositis and alopecia. Since the drugs act on immune cells, they are also used for autoimmune diseases including [[Rheumatoid arthritis]], [[Lupus|systemic lupus erythematosus]] and [[Multiple sclerosis]].

City (pop., 2020: 20,937,757), capital of [[Sichuan]] province, China. It is the fourth most populous city in China and traditionally the hub of Western China. Founded by the Kingdom of Shu in the 4th century BC, it is the only Chinese settlement to have kept its name unchanged through the imperial, republican and communist eras. It was capital of Liu Bei's Shu Han Empire during the [[Three Kingdoms]] era. Its economy spans machinery, automobile, medical, food and [[Information technology|information technology]] industries, and it is a leading financial hub. The city is the seat of the Western Theater Command of the [[People's Liberation Army]] and home to the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding. The Dujiangyan irrigation system is a [[World Heritage Site]], and in 2011 [[UNESCO]] recognized the city as a city of gastronomy.

Capital and largest city of [[Tamil Nadu]], southern India, on the Coromandel Coast of the [[Bay of Bengal]]. Known as Madras until it was officially renamed Chennai in 1996, it is the sixth-most-populous city in India as of the 2011 census. The British [[East India Company]] obtained a coastal land grant in 1639 and built Fort St. George, the first British fortress in India, and by the late 18th century the British had established the Madras Presidency. Chennai is a major center for music, art and dance and is called the Cultural Capital of South India; it was added to the [[UNESCO]] Creative Cities Network in October 2017. It has a [[Tropical climate|tropical climate]] with high [[Humidity|humidity]], and most rain falls in the [[Monsoon|northeast monsoon]].

Written order to a [[Bank|bank]] to pay a specific sum from a person's account to a named payee. The drawer writes the amount, date and payee and signs the check, ordering the drawee bank to pay. Forms of checks have existed since ancient times and at least since the 9th century, but they became a popular non-cash payment method in the 20th century, and volumes peaked in or around the early 1990s. Since then, [[Debit card|debit cards]], [[Credit card|credit cards]] and mobile payments have replaced them, and in an increasing number of countries checks are marginal or phased out. In the [[Maurya Empire]] of India (321–185 BC), an order called the *adesha* told a banker to pay money to a third person. The spelling *check* is standard in [[American English]].

American singer and actress, dubbed the "Goddess of Pop." She rose to fame in 1965 as part of the folk rock duo Sonny & Cher. Her album *Believe* (1998) introduced the "Cher effect," a stylized use of Auto-Tune, and its title track was the number-one song in the United States in 1999. She won an Academy Award for Best Actress for *Moonstruck* and is the only performer to have won an Academy Award for acting and been inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]]. She has sold over 100 million records.

Electromagnetic radiation emitted by a charged particle moving through a [[Dielectric|dielectric medium]] faster than light travels in that medium, as in the blue glow of an underwater nuclear reactor. Its cause is similar to that of a [[Sonic boom|sonic boom]]. Named after Soviet physicist Pavel Cherenkov, who first detected it experimentally in 1934, it was explained by Igor Tamm and Ilya Frank in 1937 within [[Special relativity|special relativity]]; the three shared the 1958 Nobel Prize in Physics. Particle detectors use its emission angle to measure particle speed.

Nuclear accident at Reactor 4 of the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant, near Pripyat in the Ukrainian SSR of the [[Soviet Union]], on April 26, 1986. Operators were running a safety test after an accidental drop in reactor power, and design flaws led to a power surge, steam explosions and a meltdown, followed by a core fire that dispersed radioactive contaminants across the Soviet Union and [[Europe]]. The government set up an exclusion zone, later expanded to 30 km in radius, and around 49,000 people were initially evacuated, with approximately 68,000 more later. Of 237 hospitalized workers, 134 showed symptoms of acute radiation syndrome and 28 died within three months. It is one of only two nuclear accidents rated at the maximum severity on the International Nuclear Event Scale, the other being the [[Fukushima nuclear accident]].

Indigenous people of the Southeastern Woodlands of the [[United States]], whose language belongs to the Iroquoian family. Before the 18th century they lived in river-valley towns in what are now [[North Carolina]], Tennessee, Virginia, South Carolina, Georgia and Alabama, with hunting grounds reaching into [[Kentucky]]. [[Sequoyah]] devised a syllabary in the early 1820s, enabling rapid literacy and the publication of the *Cherokee Phoenix* newspaper. Under the Indian Removal Act of 1830, many Cherokee were forced west, with federal troops marching approximately 16,000 westward along the [[Trail of Tears]]; about 4,000 died from disease, exposure and starvation. Today three tribes are federally recognized: the Cherokee Nation and the United Keetoowah Band, both in Oklahoma, and the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians in North Carolina.

Fleshy drupe, or stone fruit, of many plants in the genus *Prunus*. Commercial cherries come from [[Cultivar|cultivars]] of the sweet cherry (*Prunus avium*) and the sour cherry (*Prunus cerasus*). The indigenous range of the sweet cherry extends through most of Europe, western Asia and parts of northern Africa, and the fruit has been eaten there since prehistoric times. Cherries were introduced into England at Teynham, near Sittingbourne in [[Kent]], by order of [[Henry VIII]], who had tasted them in [[Flanders]]. Irrigation, spraying and labor make cherries relatively expensive, and sour cherries need no pollenizer, while few sweet varieties are self-fertile.

American stage and screen actress. A founding member of the American Repertory Theater in 1980, she won two Tony Awards for Best Actress in a Play, for *The Heiress* (1995) and *Doubt* (2005). She has won three Primetime Emmy Awards, one of them in 2009 for her role as President Allison Taylor in *24*. Her television work also includes Barbara Layton in *The West Wing*, and her films include *Erin Brockovich* (2000) and *The Village* (2004).

Flower of ornamental [[Cherry|cherry]] trees in the subgenus *Cerasus*, called *sakura* in Japanese. The blossom is the national flower of Japan and central to *hanami*, the custom of flower viewing that dates to at least the [[Heian period]]. Most ornamental trees are [[Cultivar|cultivars]] of wild species, and many derive from *Prunus speciosa*; cultivars of this group have been produced since the 14th century. Japan presented trees to the [[United States]] in 1912 as a token of friendship, and ornamental planting spread to Europe and the United States in the early 20th century.

Hard, fine-grained [[Sedimentary rock|sedimentary rock]] composed of microcrystalline or cryptocrystalline [[Quartz|quartz]]. It is characteristically of biological origin, formed from the remains of siliceous ooze containing [[Diatom|diatoms]] and radiolarians; Precambrian cherts preserve fossil [[Cyanobacteria|cyanobacteria]]. Where chert occurs in chalk or marl, it is usually called [[Flint|flint]]. Its colors range from white to black, most often gray, brown and light green to rusty red, and red and green are usually related to iron. Most cherts are nearly pure silica, with less than 5% other minerals.

Ceremonial county in northwest England (pop., 2024: 1,139,884). Covering 2,344 sq km, it borders [[Wales]] to the west, [[Greater Manchester]] to the north-east and Derbyshire to the east. Its largest settlement is Warrington, and the city of Chester lies in the west. The landscape is dominated by the flat Cheshire Plain, and red [[Triassic]] [[Sandstone|sandstone]] underlies much of the county and was used in many of its buildings. The name derives from Chester and was recorded in the [[Domesday Book]] as Cestrescir.

Traditional [[Board game|board game]] for two players, played on an 8×8 grid of 64 squares. Each side controls sixteen pieces, and the objective is to checkmate the enemy king. Recorded history begins with chaturanga in 7th-century [[India]], and modern rules emerged in [[Europe]] at the end of the 15th century. The first universally recognized world champion, Wilhelm Steinitz, claimed the title in 1886, and international competition is governed by the International Chess Federation (FIDE). In 1997 Deep Blue became the first computer to win a match against a reigning World Champion, defeating [[Garry Kasparov]]. Modern engines are significantly stronger than human players, but chess is not a solved game.

Deciduous tree or shrub of the genus *Castanea* in the beech family, Fagaceae, native to temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere. The name also refers to the edible nuts the trees produce. The European sweet chestnut (*Castanea sativa*) can reach 35–36 m, and the American chestnut (*Castanea dentata*) around 30 m. Chestnut flowers are not self-compatible, so two trees are required for [[Pollination|pollination]], and each spiny burr contains one to seven nuts depending on the species. The nuts are [[Starch|starchy]] and have long been a staple food.

American automobile division of [[General Motors]], selling vehicles from subcompacts to medium-duty [[Truck|trucks]]. Founded as the Chevrolet Motor Car Company on November 3, 1911, by Louis Chevrolet, Arthur Chevrolet and William C. Durant, it was used by Durant to acquire a controlling stake in General Motors in 1918. Alfred Sloan made Chevrolet the volume leader in the General Motors family, and by 1929 it had overtaken Ford as the best-selling car in the [[United States]]. Chevrolet is sold in most automotive markets worldwide.

American comedian, writer and actor. A breakout cast member of the first season of *Saturday Night Live* (1975–1976), he anchored its recurring *Weekend Update* segment and earned two Primetime Emmy Awards as both performer and writer. He then starred in films including *Caddyshack* (1980), *Fletch* (1985) and *Spies Like Us* (1985), and played Clark Griswold in five *National Lampoon's Vacation* films. He hosted the [[Academy Awards]] in 1987 and 1988.

Capital and most populous city of [[Wyoming]] (pop., 2020: 65,132). Established in 1867 as a junction on the [[Union Pacific Railroad]] in the Dakota Territory, it was named for the Cheyenne people. Its economy is anchored by government services, transportation and military operations at Francis E. Warren Air Force Base, which began as a [[Cavalry|cavalry]] encampment. It has remained the only capital of Wyoming, and it is known for Cheyenne Frontier Days, a long-running [[Rodeo|rodeo]] and cultural event.

Landlocked state in east-central [[India]], the ninth largest by area. Formed on November 1, 2000, from the southeastern districts of [[Madhya Pradesh]], it has [[Raipur]] as its capital. The most popular theory traces the name to 36 ancient forts, and the region was consolidated under the Kingdom of Haihaiyavansi for 700 years. The Bhonsles of Nagpur ruled until the [[East India Company]] annexed the region in 1845. It has the third largest coal reserves in India, and forests cover over 41.21% of the state.

Capital and largest city of [[Moldova]] (pop., 2024: over 567,000). Moldova's main industrial and commercial center and its largest transport hub, it lies on the Bîc River, a tributary of the Dniester. Formerly known as Kishinev, it has notable architecture that includes postwar Socialist realist and Brutalist buildings. The house where [[Alexander Pushkin]] lived in exile from [[Alexander I of Russia]] is now a museum.
